newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bars Gerry Adams due to IRA links.
newsitem.headline: Australia bars Gerry Adams due to IRA links.

text.p: Australia on Friday barred Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams from entering the country because of his "intimate association" with the Irish Republican Army (IRA).

Australian Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock said he had refused Adams an entry visa because he had failed to meet the good character requirements of the Migration Act through his IRA association. Sinn Fein is the political wing of the IRA.
Adams, who has never visited Australia, had sought a visa to promote his autobiography "Before the Dawn" later this month.
"Mr Adams continues to be intimately associated with the Provisional Irish Republican Army, known as the P.I.R.A.," Ruddock said at a news conference in Sydney.
"The P.I.R.A. is an organisation that continues to conduct criminal acts of terrorism and bombing," Ruddock said. "On this basis, I have refused Mr Adams' application."

Ruddock refused to detail what he meant by Adams' "intimate association" or explain why other Sein Finn officials, such as executive member Dodie McGuiness, have been allowed to enter Australia. He also refused to say what Adams needed to do to be acceptable to the Australian government.
The Australian government has been concerned that Adams did not condemn the IRA's resumption of violence after the ceasefire breakdown on February 9.
The IRA ended its 17-month truce by attacking British targets in Britain and Germany, then struck in Northern Ireland last month with an attack on Britain's army headquarters.
Britain and Ireland, in an attempt to forge a political settlement to 27 years of the Northern Ireland conflict, say Sinn Fein cannot attend peace talks until there is a new IRA truce.

Sinn Fein's Dodie McGuinness said the decision to refuse Adams a visa was "unhelpful" at a time when Adams and nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party leader John Hume were working to restore the peace process in Northern Ireland.
U.S. President Bill Clinton's decision to grant Adams a visa in 1994 helped lead to the IRA's ceasefire later that year.

"It is universally recognised, even by the British government, that Gerry Adams has played a central role in the search for a peace settlement in Ireland," McGuiness said in a statement released here.
"He has said many times that a democratic peace settlement is his personal and political priority," McGuiness said.
"We are aware that the British government lobbied extensively against Mr Adams' trip," she said.
However, Ruddock said his decision to bar Adams was taken by him, without consultation with the British government, and based solely on Australian law.
Australian Aid for Ireland national president Michael Morgan said the ban brought into question the Australian government's political independence and its commitment to free speech.

"This decision is a confused and ill-informed one which makes no positive contribution in the quest for peace in Ireland," Morgan said in a statement. There are about 55,000 Irish-born Australians in the nation's 18 million population.
"It also highlights to the world at large the lack of independent political vision on the part of the ... government and a mirror image of British government opinion."
Australian Prime Minister John Howard said Adams was the head of Sinn Fein, "the political mouthpiece of a terrorist organisation", and his ban had nothing to do with free speech.

Morgan also said the visa ban could embarrass newly-elected U.S. President Bill Clinton when he arrives in Australia on November 19 for a four day visit. Clinton held talks with the Sinn Fein leader in Washington in February this year.
